name: Battle of Gettysburg
info: Union forces under George Meade defeated Robert E. Lee's Confederate army at Gettysburg, Pennsylvania, from 1 to 3 July 1863, ending Lee's invasion of the North and forcing his retreat to Virginia.

facts.place: In and around Gettysburg, Pennsylvania, United States
facts.sides: Union Army of the Potomac under George G. Meade (more than 100,000 men) against the Confederate Army of Northern Virginia under Robert E. Lee (75,000 in one figure given, 72,000 in another)
facts.outcome: The Union army held its lines and repulsed Pickett's Charge; Lee's invasion of the North ended and his army retreated, crossing the Potomac on 13 and 14 July.

t: Lee invaded the North in June 1863 partly for supplies, relief for Virginia and the hope of strengthening the Northern peace movement, and the armies met by chance at Gettysburg.
The Union army held a fishhook-shaped line on interior lines through three days and turned back Pickett's Charge on 3 July.
Historians agree it was a Union victory but are divided on whether it was decisive, and the war went on for almost two more years.
dyk: Only one civilian death is documented during the battle, Ginnie Wade, yet the town of 2,400 was left to care for 14,000 wounded Union troops and 8,000 Confederate prisoners.
ev: Lee wins at Chancellorsville and decides on a second invasion of the North; his army begins to move north from Fredericksburg on 3 June
Meade replaces Hooker in command of the Army of the Potomac on 28 June
On 1 July Heth's division meets Buford's cavalry west of Gettysburg and the Union I and XI corps retreat to Cemetery Hill
On 2 July Longstreet attacks the Union left at the Peach Orchard, Devil's Den and Little Round Top; Ewell attacks Culp's Hill and East Cemetery Hill
On 3 July Pickett's Charge is repulsed at Cemetery Ridge
Lee withdraws from 4 July, the day Vicksburg surrenders; his army crosses the Potomac on 13 and 14 July
Lincoln speaks at the dedication of the Soldiers' National Cemetery on 19 November

sections.background:
The Battle of Gettysburg was fought in the American Civil War between the Union and Confederate armies, in and around Gettysburg, Pennsylvania. After the Army of Northern Virginia defeated the Army of the Potomac at Chancellorsville (30 April to 6 May 1863), General Robert E. Lee decided on a second invasion of the North. Such a move would upset the Union's summer plans, possibly ease the pressure on the besieged Confederate garrison at Vicksburg, let the army live off northern farms while war-ravaged Virginia rested, and possibly strengthen the growing peace movement in the North.

Lee's army began to move north from Fredericksburg on 3 June. After the death of Thomas J. "Stonewall" Jackson he had reorganised it into three corps under James Longstreet, Richard S. Ewell and A. P. Hill. Lee ordered his army to limit its effect on civilians, but Northern farmers and merchants were paid in virtually worthless Confederate money, and towns such as York were required to pay indemnities under threat of destruction. During the invasion the Confederates seized between 40 and nearly 60 northern African Americans; a few were escaped fugitives, but many were freemen, and all were sent south into slavery under guard.

Lee let J. E. B. Stuart take part of the cavalry around the Union army, and Stuart was absent from the army through the approach and the first two days of the battle. On 28 June Lincoln replaced Joseph Hooker with George Gordon Meade. On 1 July two brigades of Henry Heth's division advanced on Gettysburg, in what A. P. Hill meant as a reconnaissance in force.
sections.forces:
The Union Army of the Potomac, under Hooker until 28 June and then Meade, numbered more than 100,000 men. It had seven infantry corps (I, II, III, V, VI, XI and XII), a Cavalry Corps under Alfred Pleasonton and an artillery reserve; Brigadier General Henry Jackson Hunt was chief of artillery on Meade's staff. John Buford's cavalry division was the first Union force to hold the ground west of Gettysburg, fighting dismounted with breech-loading Sharps carbines. A small minority of historians write that some troopers had Spencer repeating weapons, but most sources disagree.

Lee's Army of Northern Virginia is given as 75,000 men in one passage of the source and 72,000 in another. Its three infantry corps were led by Longstreet (First), Ewell (Second) and Hill (Third), and Stuart commanded the cavalry division. Ewell and Hill, who had been division commanders under Jackson, were new to corps command.

On the first day about 22,000 of Meade's men and 27,000 of Lee's were engaged. By 2 July most of both armies had arrived. The Union line took the shape of a "fishhook" from Culp's Hill through Cemetery Hill and along Cemetery Ridge to just north of Little Round Top. The Confederate line ran about a mile to the west on Seminary Ridge and then through the town and round to a point opposite Culp's Hill, so that it was nearly five miles (8 km) long; the Union army held interior lines. Lee's plan for 2 July was a general assault, with Longstreet to attack the Union left and Ewell to attack Culp's Hill and Cemetery Hill when he heard Longstreet's guns.
sections.course:
On 1 July Buford laid out his defence on three ridges west of the town. About 7:30 a.m. Heth's brigades met his cavalry three miles west, and by 10:20 a.m. the Confederates had pushed it back to McPherson Ridge, where the vanguard of John F. Reynolds's I Corps arrived. In the afternoon Robert E. Rodes's and Jubal Early's divisions of Ewell's corps struck the Union I and XI corps from the north and north-west, and both corps retreated through the town to Cemetery Hill. Lee had told Ewell to take Cemetery Hill "if practicable"; Ewell judged an assault not practicable and did not attempt it.

On 2 July Lee's attack on the Union left began late. Daniel Sickles had moved his III Corps forward to the Peach Orchard against orders, creating a salient. Hood's and McLaws's divisions attacked just after 4 p.m. and 5 p.m., and there was fighting at Devil's Den, the Wheatfield and Little Round Top. Meade sent 20,000 reinforcements, and McLaws's attack was beaten back. About six o'clock Ewell's divisions attacked Culp's Hill and East Cemetery Hill and did not break the line.

On 3 July the second fight for Culp's Hill ended about 11 a.m.. Around 1 p.m. 150 to 170 Confederate guns began a bombardment, probably the largest of the war. About 3 p.m. between 10,500 and 12,500 Confederate soldiers advanced towards Cemetery Ridge in what is called Pickett's Charge. Fire from artillery and from Hancock's II Corps met them. The line broke briefly at the Angle and was restored. Nearly half the attackers did not return, and Pickett's division lost about two-thirds of its men.
sections.aftermath:
The two armies suffered between 46,000 and 51,000 casualties. Union casualties were 23,055 (3,155 killed, 14,531 wounded, 5,369 captured or missing). Many authors give as many as 28,000 for the Confederates; Busey and Martin (2005) document 23,231 (4,708 killed, 12,693 wounded, 5,830 captured or missing). Nearly a third of Lee's general officers were killed, wounded or captured. Between 3,000 and 5,000 horses were killed.

Only one civilian death during the battle is documented: Ginnie Wade, 20, hit by a stray bullet in her kitchen. The town, with a population of 2,400, was left to care for 14,000 wounded Union troops and an additional 8,000 Confederate prisoners. Nearly 8,000 dead needed burying quickly in the summer heat, and more than 3,000 horse carcasses were burned south of the town, which made townspeople violently ill.

On 4 July, the day the Vicksburg garrison surrendered to Ulysses S. Grant, Meade did not attack, and Lee's proposal for a prisoner exchange was rejected. Lee began to withdraw that afternoon, with a wagon train seventeen miles long carrying supplies and wounded men. At Monterey Pass on 4 July Union cavalry took 150 to 300 wagons and 1,300 to 1,500 prisoners. Swollen water and a destroyed pontoon bridge held the Confederates at the Potomac until the night of 13 July. Meade's infantry did not fully pursue until 7 July, and Lincoln and Halleck urged a harder pursuit. Lee's army crossed on 14 July, when Union cavalry took 500 prisoners and J. Johnston Pettigrew was mortally wounded.
sections.sources:
Much of what is told about the battle rests on the accounts of those who took part. Lee wrote an official report; Longstreet and Heth left memoirs; and Ewell claimed years later that Lee had changed his orders for 2 July, though this appears in neither his own nor Lee's official report. Longstreet's memoir gives his own account of what he told Lee on 3 July. Heth's memoir says that he sent Pettigrew into the town to look for supplies, especially shoes. Works on the battle include The Bachelder Papers (subtitled Gettysburg in Their Own Words), the Fremantle Diary, Haskell's account and Frassanito's study of early photography at the field, and the Official Records are available online.

Numbers are disputed. Union losses are given as 23,055, but Confederate losses are harder to establish: many authors give as many as 28,000, while Busey and Martin document 23,231. Stephen Sears puts the casualties of the whole six-week campaign at 57,225.

The causes of Lee's defeat are partisan ground. The dominant theme of the Lost Cause writers was that Lee's senior generals failed him, and they blamed his generals, Longstreet most of all, who criticised Lee in print and became a Republican after the war. Other historians hold that Lee did not manage his subordinates adequately, and most modern historians agree that both Lee and Stuart bear some responsibility for the cavalry's absence. Many historians speculate that Jackson would have taken Culp's Hill on 1 July. Whether the battle was decisive is also disputed (see Legacy).
sections.legacy:
The news electrified the North; The Philadelphia Inquirer ran the headline "Victory! Waterloo Eclipsed!" Enthusiasm faded when Lee's army escaped, and Lincoln and others criticised Meade's pursuit. Lincoln refused passage to Confederate Vice President Alexander Stephens, who approached the lines under a flag of truce, and Henry Adams wrote that all idea of European intervention was at an end. In the South Gettysburg was at first seen as a setback, not a disaster.

Historians are divided on whether the battle was decisive. Its reputation as the "turning point", usually coupled with the fall of Vicksburg, rests on the observation that Lee's army conducted no more strategic offensives. James M. McPherson wrote that Lee's army never again had the power and reputation it carried into Pennsylvania. Herman Hattaway and Archer Jones judged the strategic impact "fairly limited", and Alan Guelzo notes that the war lasted two more years. Thomas Goss and John Keegan doubt the label "decisive battle".

On 19 November 1863 Lincoln spoke at the dedication of the Soldiers' National Cemetery, later Gettysburg National Cemetery; his Gettysburg Address, of 271 words, is widely considered one of the most famous speeches in American history. Of 72 Medals of Honor for the campaign, 64 were for the battle; the latest went posthumously to Alonzo Cushing in 2014. At the 50th anniversary reunion in 1913 at least 35,000 Union veterans and a few more than 7,000 Confederate veterans attended, according to Carol Reardon, and some re-enacted Pickett's Charge in a spirit of reconciliation.

summary: At Gettysburg in July 1863 the Union Army of the Potomac stopped Robert E. Lee's second invasion of the North after three days of fighting and some 46,000 to 51,000 casualties on both sides. Historians still dispute how decisive it was.
notes: Strength: the source gives the Confederate army as 72,000 (background) and 75,000 (opposing forces); both are reported. It gives 'more than 100,000' for the Union army and no Confederate-side total for the battle other than the first-day figures (22,000 Union, 27,000 Confederate).

Casualties: Union 23,055 is stated flatly; Confederate figures are given as 'as many as 28,000' by many authors and 23,231 by Busey and Martin. The source's table of casualties by corps is empty, so none is given.

The sources section rests on works named in the source (Lee's Official Report, Longstreet's and Heth's memoirs, Ewell's later claim, Busey and Martin, Sears, the further-reading list). The source says little about how the battle is known, so this section is thin; 'the Official Records are available online' rests on its external links list.

Left out: the Gettysburg Address's full treatment, the Little Round Top and 20th Maine story (the source calls it 'fabled'), 1st Minnesota, Armistead's high-water mark, the generals killed, Sickles's wound, cavalry fights at East and South Cavalry Fields, Brandy Station, Reynolds's death, Strong Vincent, Hancock's choice of the ground, Meade's critics in Congress, Lee's health and Lee's offer to resign on 8 August (cut for length), the Lost Cause assessments of each corps commander in full, battlefield preservation and popular culture.

Doubts: the source calls the battle 'widely considered the turning point of the war, leading to the preservation of the Union and freedom from slavery' in its lead; I did not repeat this as fact because the source's own assessment section says historians are divided. 'Nearly 8,000 had been killed outright' in the source is close to but not identical with 3,155 plus 4,708 (7,863), so I used the latter only in the sums given.
